title_en: Supreme People's Court Releases Typical Cases of Infringement of Personal Rights and Interests through Information Networks
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Typical Cases on Infringement of Personal Rights and Interests Through the Use of Information Networks

Case 1

Xu Dawen v. Song Zude and Liu Xinda — Civil Dispute over Reputation Infringement

— Mental anguish damages shall be commensurate with the degree of fault of the tortfeasor

(1) Basic Facts

At approximately 1:00 a.m. on October 18, 2008, renowned movie director Xie Jin died of sudden cardiac arrest in a hotel guest room. From October 19, 2008 to December of the same year, Song Zude published several articles on his Sina blog, Sohu blog, and Tencent blog, including "Never Die Like Xie Jin!" and "Xie Jin and Liu xx Have a Severely Brain-Damaged Illegitimate Son, Xie xx, Overseas," alleging that Xie Jin died due to a sex-induced sudden death and that Xie Jin and Liu xx had a severely brain-damaged illegitimate child overseas. From October 28, 2008 to May 5, 2009, Liu Xinda published articles on his Sohu blog and NetEase blog, including "Liu Xinda Willing to Testify in Court: Xie Jin Died from Prostitution, Why Do Rogue Websites Black-box Operate to Remove Blog Posts?", "Liu Xinda: Mei X is Indeed Li xx's Daughter, the Photo Was Taken by Me," "Song Zude's Fifteen Major Predictions Have All Come True!", and "Song Zude's 22 Accurate Predictions!", claiming that he witnessed the Xie Jin incident personally, that he went overseas and saw "Xie Jin's illegitimate child" himself, and other content. In October and November 2008, reporters from Qilu Television, Chengdu Business Daily, The Beijing News, West China City Daily, Life News of Heilongjiang Daily Newspaper Group, and Tianfu Morning Post interviewed Song Zude by phone. Song Zude stated that he had solid evidence for the aforementioned articles, and Qilu Television and the various newspapers reported accordingly. After reporters from Chengdu Business Daily learned from Song Zude that the information came from Liu Xinda, they also interviewed Liu Xinda by phone. Liu Xinda told the reporters that he had informed Song Zude and provided a description consistent with his blog content. Xu Dawen sued Song Zude and Liu Xinda for infringing on Xie Jin's reputation, requesting an order to cease the infringement, remove the blog articles, publish a public apology in relevant media, and pay RMB 100,000 in economic losses and RMB 400,000 in mental anguish damages.

(2) Judgment

The Jing'an District People's Court of Shanghai held at first instance that the registered user of a blog bears legal responsibility for the truthfulness of blog articles and has the obligation to avoid causing unlawful infringement against others. Song Zude and Liu Xinda each uploaded defamatory articles first, and Song Zude stated that the information came from Liu Xinda's "first-hand hearing and witnessing," while Liu Xinda publicly claimed that he personally heard the event and told Song Zude, through uploading blog articles and narrating to inquiring media. The two not only committed tortious acts individually but also had a meeting of minds regarding the infringement of Xie Jin's reputation, constituting joint tort. The defamatory articles were published publicly the day after Xie Jin's death, and they continued to slander Xie Jin's reputation during the subsequent verification process by newspapers and other media, demonstrating obvious subjective fault. Song Zude and Liu Xinda utilized the internet to publicly publish false statements, causing Xie Jin's reputation to be unlawfully infringed upon to a greater extent. The subjective fault of the two defendants was very serious, the tortious means were extremely despicable, and this dealt a severe blow to the physical and mental health of Xie Jin's widow, Xu Dawen. In summary, the judgment ordered Song Zude and Liu Xinda to cease the infringement, publish a statement of public apology to Xu Dawen in prominent positions in multiple print and online media to eliminate the impact, and pay Xu Dawen RMB 89,951.62 in economic losses and RMB 200,000 in mental anguish damages. Song Zude and Liu Xinda appealed but lost; the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's People's Court affirmed the original judgment and dismissed the appeal.

(3) Typical Significance

This case is one involving infringement of another person's reputation through the use of a blog. As stated in the judgments of the first and second instances, expression in self-media such as public blogs, like expression through radio, television, newspapers, and other means, must comply with national laws and regulations and must not infringe upon the lawful rights and interests of others. The blog owner bears legal responsibility for the blog content. In this case, the two defendants infringed on Xie Jin's reputation using the internet and other media. Based on factors such as the subjective fault of their conduct, the despicable nature of the tortious means, and the consequences of the tort, the court awarded a relatively high amount of mental anguish damages, reflecting the principles and spirit of the Tort Law.

Case 2

Cai Jiming v. Baidu Inc. — Dispute over Infringement of Right to Reputation, Right to Portrait, Right to Name, and Right to Privacy

— The mere appearance of infringing information shall not be deemed sufficient to determine that a network service provider knew of the existence of the tortious fact

(1) Basic Facts

After the plaintiff, as a member of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, publicly published a proposal on holiday reform, it attracted public attention. Internet users posted text and image content containing insults and defamation, as well as disclosed the plaintiff's personal mobile phone number, home phone number, and other personal information, in the "Cai Jiming Bar" opened on Baidu Tieba. Baidu Inc. stipulated the basic rules for using "Baidu Tieba" and the complaint methods and rules on the homepage of "Baidu Tieba." It provided that any user who discovers that a post in a tieba is suspected of insulting or defaming others, infringing upon the lawful rights and interests of others, or violating the tieba agreement has the right to file a complaint in accordance with the tieba complaint rules. Cai Jiming authorized Liang Wenyan to contact Baidu Inc. by phone regarding the tieba in question, but Baidu Inc. did not handle it. Liang Wenyan also applied to become an administrator of "Cai Jiming Bar" but was not approved. Later, Liang Wenyan sent a message to the tieba management team requesting the deletion of infringing posts in the bar, but the management team did not reply. On October 13, 2009, Cai Jiming authorized his lawyer to send a lawyer's letter to Baidu Inc., requesting the company to fulfill its legal obligations, delete the infringing statements, and close "Cai Jiming Bar." After receiving the lawyer's letter, Baidu Inc. deleted the allegedly infringing posts in "Cai Jiming Bar." Cai Jiming filed a lawsuit against Baidu Inc., requesting an order to delete the infringing information, close "Cai Jiming Bar," disclose the personal information of the network users who posted the infringing information, and compensate for losses.

(2) Judgment

The Haidian District People's Court of Beijing held at first instance that Baidu Tieba service is a network service that provides conditions for information publication to internet users through specific electronic interactive forms. The law does not impose on network service providers the legal obligation to review each post in a tieba. Therefore, the fact that allegedly infringing personal rights and interests appear in the electronic bulletin board service provided by a network service provider cannot naturally lead to the inference that it "knew" of the tortious fact. Pursuant to the Regulations on the Administration of Internet Electronic Bulletin Board Services, a network service provider is only required to bear the obligations of "prior notice" and "post-supervision" for infringing information posted on its electronic bulletin board platform that is suspected of infringing personal rights and interests, providing a convenient channel for rights holders to file complaints and ensuring the effectiveness of such a complaint channel. Baidu Inc. had fulfilled its statutory obligation of prior notice and post-supervision by providing an effective complaint channel and had not violated its statutory duty of care. After receiving Cai Jiming's lawyer's letter on October 15, 2009, Baidu Inc. immediately deleted the infringing information and therefore did not bear tort liability. Since Baidu Inc. had already deleted the infringing information and taken blocking measures to prevent the publication of new infringing information, Cai Jiming's continued request for Baidu Inc. to close the relevant tieba had no legal basis. Moreover, Cai Jiming, having passively become a public figure due to the publicly concerned "national holiday reform" event, became the focus of public attention. For the sake of public opinion supervision and freedom of speech, the public should be allowed to express different views through various channels, as long as malicious personal attacks or insults are not directed at Cai Jiming himself. "Cai Jiming Bar" is merely a channel for public opinion to express views on public figures and public events, and naming the bar after "Cai Jiming" only indicates the focus of public opinion. It was not intended to infringe on his right to name, so the request to close "Cai Jiming Bar" was not supported.
Regarding Cai Jiming's pre-litigation request to Baidu Inc. for disclosure of the personal information of the relevant network users, Baidu Inc., in accordance with Article 15 of the Regulations on the Administration of Internet Electronic Bulletin Board Services, did not directly provide the infringing network user information to Cai Jiming and was not at fault. During the lawsuit, Cai Jiming requested that Baidu Inc. provide the above information, and Baidu Inc. stated in court that it could technically provide it. Therefore, Cai Jiming's request that Baidu Inc. provide the personal information of the allegedly infringing network users through the court was justified, and the court of first instance supported this request.
The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held at second instance that Baidu Inc. failed to take timely measures after receiving Liang Wenyan's complaint, and only took measures such as deleting information after Cai Jiming sent a formal lawyer's letter. During the period between Liang Wenyan's complaint and Cai Jiming's formal lawyer's letter, Baidu Inc. neglected its post-management obligations, thereby expanding the damage caused by the network users' infringement on Cai Jiming. Therefore, Baidu Inc. should bear corresponding tort liability. Based on the specific circumstances of this case, Baidu Inc. was ordered to pay Cai Jiming RMB 100,000 in mental anguish damages.

(3) Typical Significance

This case concerns the issue of the boundary of liability for network service providers and provides reference in three aspects: First, the method and effect of the notifier's notice is related to the method published by the network service provider. As long as the notifier satisfies the notification method published by the network service provider, the network service provider shall take necessary measures. The court of second instance held that Baidu Inc. should bear responsibility for the period between the complaint made by the plaintiff's authorized agent and the delivery of the plaintiff's lawyer's letter, which is based on this premise. Second, in determining whether a network service provider knew that a network user infringed upon the rights and interests of others through its service, it cannot be presumed that it "knew" merely because infringing facts appear in the services it provides. Third, attention should be paid to balancing the supervision and expression freedom regarding public figures with infringement, achieving a balance between the two. The courts of first and second instance properly balanced the interests by not supporting the request to delete "Cai Jiming Bar".

Case 3

Beijing Jinshan Security Software Co., Ltd. v. Zhou Hongyi — Dispute over Infringement of Reputation

— Public figures shall bear a greater duty of care when publishing online statements

(1) Basic Facts

Between May 25 and May 27, 2010, Zhou Hongyi (Chairman of Qizhi Software (Beijing) Co., Ltd.) published multiple blog posts on his Sina Weibo, Sohu Weibo, NetEase Weibo, and other microblogs, with content including "Uncovering Jinshan Company's Mask," "The MicroPoint Case," "Jinshan Software Destroys 360 Security Guard," and others. Jinshan Company claimed that these microblogs fabricated facts, maliciously defamed it, and damaged its business reputation and product reputation. The content was reported by online and print media, resulting in a decrease in Jinshan Company's social evaluation. Therefore, Jinshan Company requested Zhou Hongyi to cease the infringement, publish a letter of apology on the homepages of Sina, Sohu, and NetEase microblogs, and compensate for economic losses of RMB 12 million.

(2) Judgment

The Haidian District People's Court of Beijing held at first instance that the characteristic of microblogs is their brevity and instant expression of feelings and thoughts about people and things, serving as an emotional platform for self-sharing. Compared to formal media, statements on microblogs are more casual and subjective, and the latitude for freedom of speech is broader. Considering the "self-media" nature of microblogs with an unspecified and wide-reaching audience, the determination of whether a microblog statement constitutes infringement should take into account the specific identity of the speaker, specific content of the statement, relevant context, specific circumstances of the audience, and the specific consequences caused or likely to be caused by the statement. Zhou Hongyi, as the Chairman of Qihoo 360, a competitor of Jinshan Company, and a verified "V" public figure on Sina Weibo with a larger audience and greater influence, should bear a greater duty of care than ordinary persons. When publishing commentary statements about competitors, he should exercise more restraint to avoid damaging their business reputation. The court of first instance held that Zhou Hongyi used his microblog as a platform for "microblog marketing" and intensively published improper and unreasonable evaluations of Jinshan Software. His purpose was to weaken Jinshan's competitive ability by damaging its business reputation and product reputation, thereby giving his own company a competitive advantage. He had subjective intent to commit tort, and his conduct inevitably led to a decrease in Jinshan Company's social evaluation, infringing upon its reputation. He should bear liability to cease the infringement, apologize, eliminate the impact, and compensate for losses. However, Jinshan Company presented no evidence proving a causal link between the drop in its stock price and Zhou Hongyi's microblog statements. The court ordered Zhou Hongyi to cease infringement, delete the relevant microblog posts, publish a letter of apology on the homepages of Sina, Sohu, and NetEase microblogs, and pay RMB 80,000 in economic damages. The court of second instance modified this to RMB 50,000 in economic damages.

(3) Typical Significance

This case involves infringement of an enterprise's reputation through the use of microblogs. First, the courts of first and second instance, considering the characteristics of microblogs as "self-media," held that the standard for determining whether microblog statements constitute infringement should be relatively relaxed, reflecting a judicial approach aligned with internet technology development, which is commendable. Second, both courts held that whether microblog statements constitute infringement should be determined by comprehensively considering factors such as the blogger's identity, the content of the statements, and the subjective purpose. Public figures should bear a greater duty of care, a judgment consistent with the basic principles of tort law. This case is particularly instructive against the backdrop of the increasing phenomenon of using the internet to infringe upon the business reputation of business entities, or the social evaluation of goods or services.

Case 4

Zhao Yazhi v. Shanghai Qizi Trading Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Nuobaosi Cosmetics Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Infringement of Right to Name and Right to Portrait

— The influence of the injured party is an important factor in determining economic losses

(1) Basic Facts

On May 16, 2005, Zhao Yazhi and Nuobaosi Company entered into an "Image Endorsement Agreement," stipulating that Zhao Yazhi allowed Nuobaosi Company to legally use her portrait for advertising and promotion of VZI series cosmetics, with the contract effective from July 31, 2005 to July 31, 2006, and Nuobaosi Company paying HKD 800,000 as remuneration. On January 9, 2012, Defendant Qizi Company and Defendant Nuobaosi Company entered into an agreement stipulating that Nuobaosi Company recognized Qizi Company as the exclusive general distributor for "VZI Oxygen Therapy Series Products" in the Shanghai region; Nuobaosi Company would provide Qizi Company with promotional materials for "VZI" products featuring brand spokesperson Zhao Yazhi and five other celebrities; the agreement was valid from January 9, 2012 to January 8, 2013. In 2012, Qizi Company used Zhao Yazhi's name and portrait on its website. Zhao Yazhi sued, requesting an order for the two defendants to cease using her name and portrait, publicly apologize, and pay RMB 950,000 in economic losses and RMB 50,000 in moral damages.

(2) Judgment

The Pudong District People's Court of Shanghai held that Nuobaosi Company, without Zhao Yazhi's consent, had no right to continue using her name and portrait after the period agreed upon in the contract expired, nor did it have the right to authorize others to use them. The conduct of the two defendants infringed upon the plaintiff's right to name and right to portrait. The plaintiff, as a film and television star, has a high level of recognition for her name and image in Mainland China. Combined with her good appearance and good reputation among the public, using her name and image for promotional purposes for related products can enhance the product's influence and credibility, bringing actual benefits to the manufacturer or seller of the product. Therefore, the plaintiff's name and portrait have certain commercial value. Infringement upon her right to name and right to portrait entitles the injured party to seek compensation for economic losses. In determining the amount, the court considered factors such as the duration of Qizi Company's use of the plaintiff's name and portrait on its website, the scope of impact on the plaintiff, and the degree of fault in its conduct, and ordered Defendant Qizi Company to compensate the plaintiff RMB 250,000 in damages, with Nuobaosi Company bearing joint and several liability.

(3) Typical Significance

Using the influence of celebrities to enhance the visibility of products or services is a common marketing technique. Based on internet technology, it is easier to verify the unauthorized use of another person's portrait or name than in the past. The characteristic of this case is that in determining the victim's economic losses, the court comprehensively considered factors such as the injured party's level of recognition, the potential to enhance the product's influence and credibility through promotion using her name and image, the actual benefits to the manufacturer or seller, the duration of unauthorized use, the scope of impact on the injured party, and the degree of fault. Based on these factors, the court awarded substantial economic damages, thereby implementing the function of the system to sanction illegal conduct and increase the cost of illegal behavior through damages.

Case 5

Fan Bingbing v. Bi Chenggong and Guizhou Yisaide Culture Media Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Infringement of Reputation

— Liability of the "Insinuator": Judgment from the Perspective of the Information Recipient

(1) Basic Facts

On May 19, 2012, Hong Kong's Apple Daily published an unverified negative report about Mainland movie star Zhang Ziyi. On May 30, 2012, Bi Chenggong forwarded and commented on a microblog he had posted on March 31, 2012. The main content suggested that the aforementioned negative report was orchestrated by "Miss F." At 19:10 on May 30, 2012, "Entertainment News" on the news section of the Qianxun website, run by Yisaide Company, published an article titled "Screenwriter Exposes Inside Story of Zhang Ziyi Being Framed, Mastermind Fan Bingbing Has No Films to Shoot," which, based on the aforementioned microblog content, stated: "...Well-known screenwriter Bi Chenggong revealed on his Sina Weibo the inside story of Zhang Ziyi being framed, stating that Fan Bingbing was the mastermind behind it. ..." Subsequently, the article published by Yisaide Company and the microblog posted by Bi Chenggong were widely forwarded and reproduced. Major portal websites such as Sina, Sohu, Tencent, and NetEase, as well as various well-known domestic newspapers, carried related reports and derivative stories, leading to a large number of insulting and attack-based comments and evaluations about Fan Bingbing online. Fan Bingbing sued, requesting an order for Yisaide Company and Bi Chenggong to cease the infringement, delete the microblog information, publicly apologize, and pay RMB 500,000 in moral damages. Bi Chenggong argued in his defense that "Miss F" referred to American actress Lily Collins, who played "Clary Fray" in the US film "The Mortal Instruments."

(2) Judgment

The Beijing Chaoyang District Court and the Second Intermediate People's Court held that, under certain circumstances, a defamatory statement may be implied in a surface statement (i.e., by insinuation). In such a case, the defamatory statement is not required to name the plaintiff by name; it is sufficient that the plaintiff proves that, under the specific circumstances, persons with a particular background of knowledge would reasonably believe that the statement was directed at the plaintiff. From the timing and background of the microblog post by Bi Chenggong, it would readily lead readers to conclude that "Miss F" was involved in the report concerning Zhang Ziyi. From the comments under Bi Chenggong's microblog post, the article "Inside Story", and the subsequent large number of netizens' comments and related reports, the majority believed that "Miss F" referred to Fan Bingbing. Although on June 4, 2012, Bi Chenggong posted a microblog stating that he did not name anyone as having defamed Zhang Ziyi, a large number of comments under that microblog still indicated that most netizens believed that Fan Bingbing was the one who carried out the alleged frame-up plan, and Bi Chenggong did not make any further clear refutation denying that "Miss F" was Fan Bingbing. The evidence submitted by Bi Chenggong failed to prove the existence of a "frame-up plan" or the relationship between Lily Collins and any such plan. Moreover, before the lawsuit, when faced with a large number of netizens believing that "Miss F" referred to Fan Bingbing, Bi Chenggong never mentioned that "Miss F" referred to Lily Collins. Therefore, Bi Chenggong's explanation of the identity of "Miss F" clearly lacked evidentiary support. Yisaide Company, as a network service provider, should bear the obligation of reviewing and verifying news published on its website "Qianxun Net". The article "Inside Story" was actively edited and published by Yisaide Company, but was not reviewed or verified beforehand. Consequently, the liability arising therefrom should be borne by Yisaide Company itself. In conclusion, Bi Chenggong and Yisaide Company should respectively bear the liability of making an apology and paying compensation for moral damages in the amounts of 30,000 yuan and 20,000 yuan.

(3) Typical Significance

In cases involving infringement of personality rights such as the right to reputation through the use of information networks, the infringing information often has the characteristics of "making insinuations" or "cursing indirectly", without clearly identifying the injured party, especially when targeting public figures. How to determine whether the target of the online information is the plaintiff? How to determine whether the plaintiff has suffered damage due to such information? The conclusion of this case is that the judgment should be made from the perspective of the recipient of the information, i.e., "the defamatory statement is not required to name the plaintiff by name; it is sufficient that the plaintiff proves that, under the specific circumstances, persons with a particular background of knowledge would reasonably believe that the statement was directed at the plaintiff." This standard of judgment substantively captures the consequence of damage and the causal relationship between the consequence of damage and the infringing information, providing enlightening significance for the adjudication of cases involving infringement of the right to reputation through the use of network information.

Case 6

Wang v. Zhang, Beijing Lingyun Interactive Information Technology Co., Ltd., and Hainan Tianya Online Network Technology Co., Ltd. — series of disputes over infringement of right to reputation

Media reports should respect personal privacy

(1) Basic Facts

Wang and the deceased Jiang were husband and wife, having registered their marriage on February 22, 2006. On December 29, 2007, Jiang committed suicide by jumping from the 24th floor of the building where she lived.

Before her death, Jiang registered a personal blog under the name "The Migratory Bird Flying North" on the internet and wrote on it. Two months before her suicide, Jiang closed her blog, but had been recording, in diary form on the blog, her mental journey during those two months, posting a photo of Wang together with a woman surnamed Dong (who was not a party to the case) on the blog, believing that the two had an improper extramarital relationship and that her marriage was a failure. Jiang's diary revealed her husband Wang's name, work unit address, and other information. On December 27, 2007, when Jiang first attempted suicide, she disclosed her blog password to a netizen and asked that netizen to open the blog 12 hours later. After Jiang committed suicide by jumping on December 29, 2007, that netizen told Jiang's sister the password, and the sister opened Jiang's blog. Zhang was a college classmate of Jiang. After learning of Jiang's death, Zhang registered a non-commercial website on January 11, 2008, with the same name as Jiang's blog, i.e., "The Migratory Bird Flying North" (URL: http://orionchris.cn/). On the homepage of this website, Zhang introduced it as "a place to mourn Jiang and to seek justice for Jiang." Zhang, as well as relatives and friends of Jiang, successively posted articles commemorating Jiang on the website. Zhang also linked the website to Tianya Net and Sina Net.

Jiang's blog diary was reposted on the Tianya Community Forum, and subsequently continuously reposted by other netizens on various websites. The circumstances of Jiang's death and Wang's "extramarital affair" triggered prolonged and sustained attention and commentary from numerous netizens. Many netizens believed that Wang's "extramarital affair" was one of the causes contributing to Jiang's suicide; while commenting, some netizens initiated "human flesh searches" against Wang on websites such as Tianya Virtual Community, gradually disclosing detailed personal information such as Wang's name, work unit, and home address; moreover, some netizens verbally abused and personally attacked Wang on websites such as Daqi Net, and some even went to Wang's home address to harass him, painting and posting slogans such as "you drove a virtuous wife to death" and "a life for a life" on his door.

Daqi Net is a commercial website registered and managed by Lingyun Company. After Jiang's death attracted widespread attention, Daqi Net created a special webpage titled "The Last BLOG Diary of the Girl Who Jumped from the 24th Floor" on January 14, 2008, which mainly included the following content: an introduction to the circumstances of Jiang's suicide; links to related posts; scenes of netizens spontaneously gathering to mourn at the community where Jiang committed suicide; on-site interviews with netizens; telephone interviews with Jiang's sister, Jiang's classmate Zhang, and the family's lawyer; and columns such as "Netizen Messages" and "Psychologist Analysis." Daqi Net used the real names of Wang, Jiang, and Dong in the special webpage, and affixed photos of Jiang, the group photo of Wang and Dong, photos of netizens spontaneously mourning at the location of Jiang's suicide, and photos of netizens harassing Wang at his doorstep and painting slogans.

Wang separately sued Zhang, Lingyun Company, and Tianya Online, requesting cessation of infringement, deletion of information, elimination of adverse effects, apology, and compensation for moral damages.

(2) Judgment

The Beijing Chaoyang District Court held that a citizen's personal emotional life, including extramarital relationships, constitutes personal privacy. Zhang's act of disclosing Wang's personal information infringed upon Wang's right to privacy. Lingyun Company, in its special webpage report on Daqi Net, failed to technically process the parties' names, personal information, and photos, thereby infringing upon Wang's right to privacy and causing damage to Wang's right to reputation. Lingyun Company should bear tort liability, including deleting the special webpage, making an apology, and compensating for moral damages. Tianya Company, which operates the Tianya Virtual Community website, had established internet usage rules in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, set up corresponding monitoring and review filtering measures for posted text, and upon learning of illegal or infringing speech online, deleted relevant network information related to this case. Tianya Company had fulfilled its regulatory obligations and should not bear tort liability.

(3) Typical Significance

What information constitutes personal information? What personal information constitutes personal privacy? Should personal information that violates public order and good customs be protected? The answers to these questions have undergone profound changes with the advent of the internet era. This case is known as the first case of blog suicide, which once attracted widespread public attention. In this case, although the plaintiff Wang's extramarital affair was morally condemnable, this did not constitute a legitimate reason for the public to intervene in his personal life. A citizen's personal emotional life, including extramarital relationships, constitutes personal privacy. Whether individuals disclose such information through the internet or the media publicly reports it, attention must be paid to protecting personal privacy.

Case 7

Yan v. Beijing Sina Internet Information Services Co., Ltd. and Beijing Baidu Netcom Science and Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of right to reputation and right to privacy

The plaintiff has the right to request the network service provider to provide relevant personal information of the infringer through litigation

(1) Basic Facts

A blogger on Sina Blog published an article involving the plaintiff's personal privacy. The plaintiff successively sent lawyer's letters to Sina Company and Baidu Company requesting them to take necessary measures. During the litigation, Sina Company did not submit evidence proving that it had taken necessary measures such as deletion, while Baidu Company provided evidence proving that it had taken measures such as disconnecting links and deleting content. The plaintiff sued requesting both companies to provide the blogger's personal information.

(2) Judgment

The Beijing Haidian District Court held that Sina Company could not prove that it had fulfilled the obligation of prior warning and subsequent supervision as required by the Provisions on the Administration of Internet Electronic Bulletin Board Services, and should bear the corresponding adverse legal consequences. Baidu Company had, on the Baidu website homepage, the "Baidu Knows" homepage, and the "Baidu Baike" homepage, publicly displayed the complaint channels and complaint procedures for rights holders, set up complaint links and rights statements, and clearly reminded netizens of their duty of attention. Baidu Company had fulfilled its statutory obligation of prior warning and subsequent supervision by providing effective complaint channels, and should not bear tort liability. Sina Company failed to prove that it had taken necessary measures after receiving the plaintiff's notification, and should bear tort liability; Baidu Company, upon receiving the plaintiff's notification, had timely taken measures such as disconnecting links and deleting content, and should not bear tort liability. The plaintiff requested Sina Company to provide the blogger's IP address and all registration information, including but not limited to name, address, contact information, and other materials. Since the content of the two blogs involved the plaintiff's personality rights and interests, the plaintiff had the right to know the personal information of the network user in order to assert his rights. Sina Company should, within the technical capabilities of the network, disclose the network user information of the aforementioned two bloggers to the plaintiff, in order to safeguard the plaintiff's right to information for the protection of his own legitimate rights and interests. This request was supported.

(3) Typical Significance

One major characteristic of network infringement cases is the anonymity of the network. How to determine the personal identity of the infringer often becomes an obstacle hindering the plaintiff from asserting his rights. On the other hand, internet companies have a statutory duty of confidentiality towards network users. How to balance the relationship between the two? Through litigation, the people's court can review and make a judgment on the plaintiff's request for the network service provider to provide the network user's personal information, thereby achieving a better balance between the two.

Case 8

Xu Jie'ao v. Beijing Sina Internet Information Services Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of right to reputation

Liability of the republisher: Professional media should bear a higher duty of care

(1) Basic Facts

On November 14, 2003, the Huashang Morning Post published an article titled "Using False Evidence, Citizen Sues Government, Fraud Exposed"; on the same day, Beijing Sina Internet Information Services Co., Ltd. republished the above article on its website, and the article remained there for as long as eight years. A separate effective judgment held that the Huashang Morning Post had infringed upon Xu Jie'ao's right to reputation and ordered it to pay 20,000 yuan in compensation for moral damages. On June 9, 2006, the Huashang Morning Post published an apology to Xu Jie'ao in a narrow column at the end of the last page of that day's newspaper, but the number of words and the space allocated were too small and not very conspicuous. Xu Jie'ao requested Sina Company to bear tort liability on the ground that it had failed to make corrections in a timely manner.

(2) Judgment

The Beijing Haidian District Court held that Sina Company's act of republishing the infringing article from the Huashang Morning Post on its website was not improper. However, after the court, at the end of 2004, determined that the Huashang Morning Post's conduct constituted infringement of the plaintiff's right to reputation, and after June 9, 2006, when the Huashang Morning Post published an apology in the newspaper, Sina Company still failed to correct or delete the information. However, because the apology published by the Huashang Morning Post was too small in space and placed in an inconspicuous position, Sina Company, although lacking subjective malice, was negligent and should bear corresponding civil liability. The amount claimed by the plaintiff was clearly excessive. The court should, based on the specific circumstances of the case, the degree of Sina Company's fault in the infringement, the duration, and other factors, determine that Sina Company compensate the plaintiff for economic losses in the amount of 80,000 yuan and moral damages in the amount of 20,000 yuan.

(3) Typical Significance

The development and maturation of self-media is a major feature of the internet era. However, this does not mean that professional media and self-media should be treated equally. The judgment in this case illustrates that when determining the legal liability for the most common act of republishing in the internet era, a distinction should be made between professional media and non-professional media, and the duty of care of professional media should be higher than that of ordinary self-media. Therefore, republishing information from others without correction still requires bearing tort liability.
